name: OPC UA
verifiedAgainst: Inductive Automation Ignition 8.3.9, secured and signed in
summary: Prefer this one when a device offers a choice. It browses, it is properly secured, and it subscribes.

addressExamples.means: Good. The namespace URI is part of the model and does not move.
Works until it doesn't. The index depends on load order.

trap: A namespace index is assigned in whatever order the server happens to load its namespaces. Add a namespace, upgrade firmware, and index 3 quietly becomes something else, so every reading is wrong with no error anywhere.
body: The driver subscribes rather than polls. The server sends a value when it changes, at a rate it can sustain, instead of being asked the same question every scan by a client with no idea whether anything moved. If a server refuses a subscription, the driver falls back to batched reads rather than failing the device.
Address nodes by namespace URI. Browse returns the URI form for exactly this reason, because the URI does not move when a server reloads.

A bare string is rejected as an address. The underlying library would happily read Temperature as ns=0;s=Temperature, which means a typo parses cleanly into a node that does not exist and the tag reads bad forever. An explicit form is required, so the mistake surfaces when you save it.

name: Modbus TCP/RTU
verifiedAgainst: A real Modbus server, run in-process, over TCP
summary: The 1979 workhorse. PLCs, VFDs, power meters, RTUs, and the fallback of every gateway that has nothing better.

addressExamples.means: A float across registers 100 and 101, word-swapped.

trap: Word order is the setting people get wrong, and a float read with the wrong order is not obviously wrong on a screen. It is a plausible number that is not the truth.
body: All four word orders are supported, under the names vendor manuals print: ABCD, CDAB, BADC, and DCBA. Set a device default with byteOrder and override it per tag with the fourth address field.

Addressing is raw and zero-based. If your drawings use the traditional 40001-style numbering, set oneBased to true and write the numbers from the drawings. Getting this wrong by one is the oldest Modbus bug there is.

Reads are merged into blocks, so adjacent and near-adjacent registers become one request. maxGap controls how many unused registers are worth reading to avoid a second round trip (default 8), and maxBlock caps a single request (default 120, protocol ceiling 125).
Writing a single bit of a holding register is a read-modify-write, because Modbus has no atomic bit-set there. The other fifteen bits are preserved.

name: MQTT and Sparkplug B
verifiedAgainst: Eclipse Mosquitto 2.0, with crafted Tahu frames
summary: Plain MQTT, or Sparkplug B as a full primary host application.

addressExamples.means: An empty device is a node-level metric.

trap: Delivering Sparkplug messages concurrently reorders them, which makes a healthy node look like it is dropping messages and provokes a rebirth storm. Message ordering is enforced.
body: As a primary host, the driver does the things the specification asks for and most integrations skip.

It publishes a retained STATE birth with a matching will, so edge nodes can see the host drop rather than inferring it from a timeout. The Sparkplug 3.0 form (spBv1.0/STATE/<host> carrying JSON) is the default, and legacyState selects the pre-3.0 ONLINE and OFFLINE string.
It tracks the per-node rolling sequence number and asks a node to rebirth when it skips, because a gap means messages were missed and the alias table can no longer be trusted.
It requests a rebirth after its own reconnect, because a host that was away has no idea what changed while it was gone.
It matches NDEATH to NBIRTH by bdSeq, so a death certificate left over from a previous session cannot kill the current one.

name: EtherNet/IP
notVerifiedNote: EtherNet/IP has not been run against a physical PLC. Its decoding and address handling are tested thoroughly, but tested logic is not the same as a value that came off a real controller. If you are the first person to point it at real hardware, treat it as commissioning and check a known value before trusting a screen.
summary: Allen-Bradley ControlLogix, CompactLogix, and Micro820. Tags have names, so the controller can be asked what it holds.

addressExamples.means: Type taken from the tag's declared dataType.
A program-scoped tag. The colon is part of the path.

trap: CIP is strongly typed and the controller rejects a read whose declared type does not match, so the type has to come from somewhere. Unknown falls back to REAL, which most process values are.
body: The type is taken from the tag's dataType, or from a :type suffix, which wins.
Reads are batched into multi-service requests, falling back to individual reads when a batch fails, so that one bad tag path does not blind the other nineteen.

name: S7comm
notVerifiedNote: S7comm has not been run against a physical PLC. Its decoding is tested thoroughly, covering every data type, sign extension, the two-byte S7 STRING header, byte ordering, block planning, and read-modify-write for bits. But tested decoding is not the same as a value that came off a real controller. If you are the first person to point it at real hardware, treat it as commissioning and check a known value before trusting a screen.
summary: Siemens S7-300, S7-400, S7-1200, and S7-1500, over ISO-on-TCP by rack and slot.
trap: The type is required for anything wider than a byte. The protocol cannot tell you whether four bytes are a REAL or a DINT, because that is a fact about the PLC program, not about the wire.
body: Defaults to rack 0, slot 1, which is right for an S7-1200 or S7-1500. An S7-300 or S7-400 is usually slot 2.
connectType defaults to 3 (S7 Basic), so the gateway does not occupy the PG connection slot an engineer wants for TIA Portal.
There is no browse. An S7 CPU does not publish the layout of its data blocks, because that lives in the TIA Portal project.

name: MTConnect
verifiedAgainst: Golden agent documents, served over HTTP
summary: Read-only machine tool telemetry. There is no command channel in MTConnect, and this driver does not pretend otherwise.

addressExamples.means: Address by either. Agents are inconsistent about which is stable.

trap: UNAVAILABLE is the agent explicitly saying it has no reading. It becomes bad quality, not the text "UNAVAILABLE" and not zero.
body: Two details separate a working integration from a plausible one. First, UNAVAILABLE becomes bad quality rather than a string or a zero. Second, a Condition's meaning is its element name (Normal, Warning, Fault, or Unavailable), not its character data, which is usually empty.
Browse reads /probe and walks the component tree to any depth.

name: HTTP and REST
summary: The catch-all, for energy meters, environmental sensors, OEM controllers, and the REST side of a gateway that speaks something proprietary underneath.

addressExamples.means: Select an array element by a field value.

trap: These APIs love returning an unordered array of name and value objects, and indexing by position is a bug waiting for a firmware update. Select by field value instead.
body: One request serves every tag on the device. Browse walks the document and reports every scalar with the path that reaches it.

name: UniFi Network
verifiedAgainst: A real UniFi Network Application 10.6 with emulated switches and a gateway, logged in as a View Only account
A real UniFi OS Server 5.1, for the UniFi OS login
Read-only on a house Cloud Gateway Ultra and an Express 7 with real USW-Lite-8-PoE switches and a U5G Backup
summary: The plant network as a device: switches, ports, PoE, WAN failover, and clients as read-only tags. Nothing writes to a console.

addressExamples.means: A console running UniFi OS. The self-hosted Network Application is https://host:8443.
A switch port's link, one of the tags that create themselves.

trap: A WAN block can say up with a stale signal while the backup link has been unplugged for days. The driver reads the console's own health checks instead, so a dead backup reads down.
body: One login per console, reused for every read, and never more than one read every ten seconds whatever the poll interval says. Make a local View Only account on the console, because a Ubiquiti cloud account can't log in from a script.

The console's certificate is pinned. The first connect fails on purpose and shows you the key fingerprint, and you paste it in. A console with a different key is refused during the handshake, before the password goes anywhere.

Switches, ports, PoE draw, WAN links, clients, and the site's health come in as tags that create themselves as gear is adopted, and go bad quality instead of vanishing. It also listens to the console's events websocket, so a switch dropping off is in the logbook when it happens, with polling still the truth underneath.

It is read-only. Writes through the write gate, starting with the locate LED, are planned and not built, and a PoE draw above zero has not been seen on real gear yet. The screens, the topology map and the events are on the UniFi page.

name: SNMP
verifiedAgainst: net-snmp's snmpd 5.9.4 (Debian's 5.9.4+dfsg-2 package) in a container in the lab, read over v1, v2c, and v3 at every security level, over UDP and TCP. The driver is gosnmp, a different implementation.
notVerifiedHeading: Verified live against a software agent. Not read off a physical switch, UPS, or PDU.
notVerifiedNote: SNMP has not been read off a physical switch, UPS, or PDU. The agent it was proven against is net-snmp's, which is what a Linux box runs and what many appliances are built on, and it is not any vendor's firmware. Vendors differ about which MIBs they serve, how they number interfaces, and how they answer a bulk request, so treat the first read of a real device as commissioning: compare the sampled values on the integration's probe with the device's own display.
summary: Switches, UPSs, PDUs, power meters, and any Linux box running snmpd, read-only. HotLoop never sends a SET.

addressExamples.means: ifOperStatus of the interface with ifIndex 2. A table cell ends in its row's index.

trap: A wrong community answers with nothing. An SNMPv1 or v2c agent drops a request carrying a community it does not know, so a wrong community, a wrong port, a firewall, and an agent that is down all look like a timeout. HotLoop's message says all four. SNMPv3 does tell them apart: a wrong passphrase or an unknown user is refused as such.
body: Read-only, always. HotLoop never sends an SNMP SET, because a SET can change a switch's configuration, and the point of this driver is to see the plant network, not to run it.

There is no default community. `public` is how a plant's switches get read by whoever asks, so a v1 or v2c device has to be given one. The community and the v3 passphrases are stored encrypted like every other device secret.

Counters are raw. A Counter32 or Counter64 only goes up and wraps, so the tag holds what the agent sent and a rate is for whatever reads the tag. TimeTicks are hundredths of a second: the integration scales sysUpTime to seconds for you.

An object the agent does not have is a bad reading with the reason, and the others in the same request still read. Browse walks the system, interface, host resources, and load tables and names each object from the MIB that defines it. You point HotLoop at a device through the integrations flow: it asks what it needs, looks at the real device, and keeps the points you choose, with nothing armed.

name: BACnet/IP
verifiedAgainst: bacpypes3 0.0.110, an independent BACnet stack in Python, serving every object type HotLoop reads
Frames recorded off that device, decoded by tests that always run. The client is written for HotLoop from the standard and shares no code with bacpypes3.
notVerifiedHeading: Verified live against a software device. Not read off a physical controller.
notVerifiedNote: BACnet/IP has not been read off a physical controller. The device it was proven against is bacpypes3's, an independent implementation of the standard, and it is not any vendor's firmware. Vendors differ about what they put in the object list, how they answer a request that is too big, and whether they answer a unicast Who-Is at all, and HotLoop's answers to the last two are tested only against the behavior bacpypes3 has. A controller on an MS/TP trunk behind a router cannot be reached.
summary: Building controllers, meters, and thermostats on the IP network, read-only. HotLoop never writes a BACnet property.

addressExamples.means: The present value of analog input 1. ai:1 is the same.
A property other than the present value, by name.
The present value of a multi-state value.

trap: Status flags are part of the reading. An object whose fault flag is set reads bad, with the reason. One that is out of service or overridden reads uncertain, because its present value is something a person or a program put there, not a measurement.
body: Read-only, on purpose. A BACnet write lands on a commandable output through a priority array, and a priority left set holds the equipment where it was put after whoever set it has gone home. That is a feature to design deliberately, not one to leave lying around.

Connecting asks the device who it is: a unicast Who-Is, and the device instance from the I-Am. A device that does not answer one is asked for its own device object under the wildcard instance. Set `deviceInstance` and a different device answering at a reused address, or a swapped controller, is refused instead of read.

ReadPropertyMultiple answers each property on its own, so an object that is not there fails its tag and no other. Nothing is segmented: a device whose answer will not fit one frame is asked for half as many objects at a time.

Routing is not built. HotLoop talks to a device it can send a UDP datagram to, so a controller on an MS/TP trunk behind a BACnet router is not reachable. Address the router's own BACnet/IP side, or put a gateway in front. You point HotLoop at a device through the integrations flow, and nothing it makes is armed.

name: Everything else
summary: Eight protocols with no driver, by choice, reached through the gateway a site already has.
body: PROFINET, EtherCAT, HART, DNP3, FINS, MELSEC/SLMP, CANopen, and FANUC FOCAS are not spoken natively, and there is no driver for them. That is a deliberate choice, not a gap waiting to be filled with a stub.

Sites running these protocols almost always already have a gateway that re-publishes on OPC UA or Modbus, such as a PROFINET IO controller with an OPC UA server, or a HART multiplexer with a Modbus map. Point a device at that endpoint and configure it as OPC UA or Modbus.

Writing eight more drivers that each duplicate what a site's existing gateway already does would add eight more things to get subtly wrong, for protocols where the equipment is hardest to test against. If a site genuinely has no gateway and needs one of these natively, that is a real piece of work to schedule, not a file to add that logs "not implemented".

There are no placeholder drivers in the tree. A protocol either has a working implementation or it is on this page. The previous version of this product had sixteen protocol files, of which fifteen returned "not implemented" while the catalog advertised all sixteen. A test now enforces that every protocol the model declares has a driver compiled in, and vice versa.
